The Eastern bettong (Bettongia gaimardi) exhibits a fascinating reproductive strategy that aligns with its role as a mycophagous marsupial, heavily dependent on hypogeous fungi. Field studies conducted in its native Tasmanian sclerophyll forests have documented that females typically produce three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year], with each litter consisting of a single pup [N_R_i = each litter consisting of a single pup], a pattern that reflects the species' slow life history and the energetic constraints of a specialized diet. This annual reproductive output is sustained across the typical breeding season and is closely tied to thermoregulatory demands; all measurements reported here were recorded from individuals maintained at a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The gestation time for this species is remarkably brief, lasting only 20 days [tg = 20 days] under these standard thermal conditions, a value that is among the shortest recorded for any macropodoid of comparable body mass at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This rapid gestation is characteristic of marsupials, where the majority of developmental investment occurs post-partum within the pouch environment.

At parturition, the altricial neonate possesses a remarkably small wet weight of just 0.307 grams [Wwb = 0.307 grams], a value that underscores the extreme altriciality of the newborn marsupial pup. This minuscule joey, no larger than a jellybean, must immediately undertake an arduous climb from the birth canal to the teat, where it will spend the next several months in continuous attachment. The subsequent developmental trajectory is one of sustained, rapid growth within the protective confines of the pouch. For comparative context, this neonatal body mass represents less than 0.02 percent of the ultimate adult body mass, highlighting the dominant role of lactation in supporting the species' growth and development. The initial weight at birth is a critical datum for understanding the species' overall life-history strategy, as it sets the stage for the extensive period of maternal investment that follows in the pouch and during the subsequent weaning phase.

The prolonged period of pouch life and subsequent weaning is a defining feature of bettong development. Under controlled conditions reflecting the species' thermoneutral zone at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 161 days [tx = 161 days]. At this developmental milestone, the young bettong, now fully furred and capable of independent locomotion, reaches a wet weight at weaning of 789 grams [Wwx = 789 grams]. This represents a substantial increase from the birth weight, achieved entirely through maternal milk provisioning. The weaning process coincides with the young transitioning to a diet of fungi, tubers, and invertebrates. A wet weight of 789 grams [Wwx = 789 grams] at this juncture is a critical threshold, as it must be sufficient to allow the juvenile to navigate its environment and locate patchily distributed food resources with a degree of independence, while still benefiting from proximity to its mother for protection and social learning.

Sexual maturation in Bettongia gaimardi requires a considerable investment in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive capability. Long-term monitoring of known-age individuals in a wild population has determined that the time since birth at puberty is 252 days [tp = 252 days] when measured against the species' standard metabolic temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This means that females are capable of conceiving their first litter at approximately eight months of age, although first successful reproduction may be delayed by environmental conditions. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults is 1729 grams [Wwi = 1729 grams], a value that typically represents the asymptote of the growth curve for this species. This adult body mass is modest relative to other bettong species, and it is associated with a life span, under these same standard thermal conditions, of approximately 4307 days [am = approximately 4307 days], which is equivalent to roughly 11.8 years at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a mammal of this size and is likely linked to its low-fecundity, high-survival life-history strategy.

The relatively long maximum life span and late maturation of the Eastern bettong are characteristic of a 'slow' life-history pace, which is also reflected in its annual reproductive rate. The capacity of females to achieve three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year] with a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] results in a maximum possible annual output of three offspring. This is a modest reproductive rate compared to many small eutherian mammals, but it is typical for medium-sized marsupials that invest heavily in each offspring. The ultimate wet weight of 1729 grams [Wwi = 1729 grams] is achieved only after the individual has passed through the vulnerable juvenile and sub-adult stages, a process that requires the successful navigation of the post-weaning period. The species' life history is thus finely tuned to the reliable, if diffuse, food resources of the fungal network, favoring adult survival and repeated, low-investment reproductive events over a strategy of high fecundity and early mortality.
